title: Trigonometry
tagline: Trigonometric ratios, identities, angles of elevation and depression, and applications to heights and distances.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Trigonometry is the study of the relationship between the sides and angles of a right-angled triangle. The three primary trigonometric ratios — sine, cosine, and tangent — are defined for an acute angle in a right triangle. This chapter also covers the reciprocal ratios (cosec, sec, cot), standard trigonometric identities, trigonometric ratios of complementary angles, and the application of trigonometry to solve problems involving angles of elevation, angles of depression, and finding heights and distances. Angles are measured in degrees, and calculations typically use π/180 for radian conversion where needed.

learningOutcomes: Define the six trigonometric ratios for an acute angle in a right triangle.
State and prove the three Pythagorean identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.
Use the complementary angle relationships: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ.
Solve problems involving angles of elevation and angles of depression.
Find the height of an object or the distance between two objects using trigonometric ratios and angles of elevation/depression.
Calculate trigonometric ratios for standard angles: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°.
Verify and apply trigonometric identities to simplify expressions and solve equations.

blocks.text: Consider a right-angled triangle with the right angle at C. Let the side opposite angle θ be the Opposite side, the side adjacent to angle θ (but not the hypotenuse) be the Adjacent side, and the side opposite the right angle (the longest side) be the Hypotenuse. The six trigonometric ratios for angle θ are defined as follows: sin θ = Opposite / Hypotenuse, cos θ = Adjacent / Hypotenuse, tan θ = Opposite / Adjacent, cosec θ = Hypotenuse / Opposite (reciprocal of sin), sec θ = Hypotenuse / Adjacent (reciprocal of cos), cot θ = Adjacent / Opposite (reciprocal of tan). These definitions apply only when θ is an acute angle (0° < θ < 90°) in a right triangle.
A right triangle labelled with angle θ, opposite side, adjacent side, and hypotenuse.

items: The hypotenuse is always the longest side and is opposite the right angle.
The opposite and adjacent sides depend on which angle θ is being considered.
cosec, sec, and cot are reciprocals of sin, cos, and tan respectively.
All ratios are positive for acute angles (0° < θ < 90°).

blocks.text: The three Pythagorean identities are derived from the Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c² applied to a right triangle with hypotenuse c and legs a, b. Dividing by c², a², or b² gives the three forms. The first and most fundamental is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. The other two are obtained by dividing by sin²θ or cos²θ, giving cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 and sec²θ − tan²θ = 1. These identities hold for all values of θ for which the expressions are defined.

items.text: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, find cos θ and tan θ.
items.note: cos θ = √(1 − sin²θ) = √(1 − 9/25) = √(16/25) = 4/5. tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = (3/5) / (4/5) = 3/4. Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, we find cos θ = 4/5 (positive since θ is acute). Then tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = 3/4.

items.text: If sec θ = 5/3, find tan θ.
items.note: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 gives tan²θ = sec²θ − 1 = (25/9) − 1 = 16/9, so tan θ = 4/3 (positive since θ is acute). Using the identity sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, we find tan²θ = 16/9, and since θ is acute, tan θ = 4/3.

items.text: Prove the identity: (cosec θ − cot θ)(cosec θ + cot θ) = 1.
items.note: LHS = cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1 (by the Pythagorean identity). = RHS. The product is a difference of squares, which simplifies to the Pythagorean identity cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1.

items: The three Pythagorean identities are: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.
These identities hold for all θ where the expressions are defined (i.e., where the denominators are non-zero).
They can be used to find one ratio given another, or to verify/trigonometric equations.
Always check the quadrant when determining the sign of a ratio; for acute angles, all ratios are positive.

blocks.text: Two angles are complementary if they sum to 90°. In a right triangle, the two acute angles are always complementary (they sum to 90°). The trigonometric ratios of complementary angles are related by co-function identities: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ. Similarly, cosec(90° − θ) = sec θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ, and cot(90° − θ) = tan θ. These identities are useful for simplifying expressions and solving problems where one angle is the complement of another.

items.text: Express sin 35° in terms of cosine of a complementary angle.
items.note: sin 35° = cos(90° − 35°) = cos 55°. Using the co-function identity sin(90° − θ) = cos θ with θ = 35°.

items.text: Express tan 50° in terms of cotangent of a complementary angle.
items.note: tan 50° = cot(90° − 50°) = cot 40°. Using the co-function identity tan(90° − θ) = cot θ with θ = 50°.

sin 25° cos 65° + sin 65° cos 25° = sin 25° cos(90° − 25°) + sin(90° − 25°) cos 25° = sin 25° sin 25° + cos 25° cos 25° = sin²25° + cos²25° = 1. Using complementary angle relationships: cos 65° = sin 25° and sin 65° = cos 25°. The expression becomes sin²25° + cos²25° = 1.

items: Complementary angles sum to 90°.
The co-function identities relate sin ↔ cos, cos ↔ sin, tan ↔ cot, cosec ↔ sec, sec ↔ cosec, cot ↔ tan.
These identities are especially useful in simplification problems and in proving other trigonometric identities.
Remember that in a right triangle, the two acute angles are always complementary.

blocks.text: The trigonometric ratios for the standard angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° are derived from the special right triangles: the equilateral triangle bisected (giving the 30-60-90 triangle and the 45-45-90 triangle). These values must be memorised, as they are used extensively in ICSE Class X problems. The complete table is: sin 0° = 0, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0; sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 45° = 1/√2, cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3; sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° is undefined.

items: Memorise these values; they are the foundation for all ICSE Class X trigonometry problems.
sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° is undefined (division by zero).
The values for 30°, 45°, 60° come from the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles.
cosec 0° and cot 0° are undefined (division by zero); sec 90° and cosec 90° are defined.

blocks.text: The angle of elevation of an object as seen by an observer is the angle between the horizontal line through the observer and the line of sight to the object (above the horizontal). The angle of depression of an object as seen by an observer is the angle between the horizontal line through the observer and the line of sight to the object (below the horizontal). In practical problems, the horizontal line is parallel to the ground, and the angle of elevation from the base of the object equals the angle of depression from the top of the object (alternate interior angles). Trigonometric ratios are used to find unknown heights, distances, or angles.

items.text: From a point on the ground 20 m from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to the top of the building is 30°. Find the height of the building.
items.note: tan 30° = height / 20, so height = 20 × tan 30° = 20 × (1/√3) = 20/√3 ≈ 11.55 m. The angle of elevation is 30°. In the right triangle, the opposite side is the building height, the adjacent side is the ground distance (20 m), and tan 30° = opposite / adjacent = 1/√3. So height = 20 × (1/√3).

items.text: From the top of a lighthouse 50 m high, the angle of depression to a boat at sea is 45°. How far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse?
items.note: tan 45° = 50 / distance, so distance = 50 / tan 45° = 50 / 1 = 50 m. The angle of depression from the top is 45°. By alternate interior angles, the angle of elevation from the boat to the top of the lighthouse is also 45°. In the right triangle, opposite = 50 m (lighthouse height), adjacent = distance from base, and tan 45° = 1 = opposite / adjacent. So distance = 50 m.

items.text: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground is 60°. From a point 20 m farther away from the tower, the angle of elevation is 30°. Find the height of the tower and the distance of the first point from the tower.
items.note: Height = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. Distance from the first point = 10 m. Let the height be h and the distance from the first point be d. From the first point: tan 60° = h / d, so h = d√3. From the second point (20 m farther): tan 30° = h / (d + 20), so h = (d + 20) / √3. Equating: d√3 = (d + 20) / √3 → 3d = d + 20 → 2d = 20 → d = 10 m. Then h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m.

items: The angle of elevation is measured above the horizontal; the angle of depression is measured below the horizontal.
The horizontal line through the observer is parallel to the ground (or the base of the object).

The angle of elevation from the base of an object equals the angle of depression from the top of the object (alternate interior angles, assuming the observer and the object are on the same horizontal plane).
Always draw a right-angled triangle marking the height, the horizontal distance, and the angle of elevation/depression.
Use the appropriate trigonometric ratio: tan for height/distance, sin for height/hypotenuse, cos for adjacent/hypotenuse.

blocks.text: This section presents full worked examples of ICSE Class X-style application problems, including finding the height of a tower, the distance between two objects, the width of a river, and problems involving two points of observation.

items.text: The shadow of a tower standing on level ground is 40 m long when the sun's altitude is 30°. Find the height of the tower.
items.note: tan 30° = height / 40, so height = 40 × tan 30° = 40 × (1/√3) = 40/√3 ≈ 23.09 m. The sun's altitude is the angle of elevation from the tip of the shadow to the top of the tower. In the right triangle, opposite = height, adjacent = 40 m (shadow), and tan 30° = 1/√3. Height = 40 × (1/√3).

items.text: From the top of a 20 m high building, the angle of depression of a car on the road is 30°. If the car is on the same level as the base of the building, how far is the car from the building?
items.note: tan 30° = 20 / distance, so distance = 20 / tan 30° = 20 / (1/√3) = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m. The angle of depression from the top of the building is 30°. By alternate interior angles, the angle of elevation from the car to the top of the building is also 30°. In the right triangle, opposite = 20 m (building height), adjacent = distance from building, and tan 30° = 1/√3. Distance = 20 / (1/√3) = 20√3.

items.text: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from point A is 30°. Moving 20 m towards the tower to point B, the angle of elevation becomes 60°. Find the height of the tower and the distance of point A from the tower.
items.note: Height = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. Distance of A from tower = 30 m. Let the height be h and the distance of A from the tower be d. From A: tan 30° = h / d, so h = d / √3. From B (20 m closer): tan 60° = h / (d − 20), so h = (d − 20)√3. Equating: d / √3 = (d − 20)√3 → d = 3(d − 20) → d = 3d − 60 → 2d = 60 → d = 30 m. Then h = 30 / √3 = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m.

items: Draw a right-angled triangle for each problem, marking the height, the horizontal distance, and the angle of elevation or depression.
The angle of elevation from the base equals the angle of depression from the top (alternate interior angles).
Use the appropriate trigonometric ratio: tan θ = opposite / adjacent is the most common for height/distanced problems.
When two observation points are given, set up two equations and solve the system by equating or subtracting.
Always check that the answer is reasonable (e.g., height must be positive, distances must be positive).

blocks.text: This section provides practice in verifying and applying trigonometric identities. The key is to start from the more complex side and use the Pythagorean identities and co-function identities to simplify to the other side.

items.text: Verify the identity: (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ.
items.note: LHS = (sin θ + cos θ)² = sin²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ + cos²θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + 2 sin θ cos θ = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ = RHS. Expand the square, use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, and simplify.

items.text: Express cosec θ in terms of cot θ, given that θ is acute.
items.note: Starting from cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, we have cosec²θ = 1 + cot²θ, so cosec θ = √(1 + cot²θ) (positive since θ is acute). Use the Pythagorean identity involving cosec and cot, then take the positive square root.

items.text: Prove: tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ.
items.note: LHS = tan θ + cot θ = sin θ / cos θ + cos θ / sin θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ) / (sin θ cos θ) = 1 / (sin θ cos θ) = (1 / sin θ)(1 / cos θ) = cosec θ sec θ = RHS. Write tan and cot in terms of sin and cos, add, use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, and recognise the reciprocals.

items: Start from the more complex side of the identity.
Use the Pythagorean identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.
Use the co-function identities for complementary angles.
Write all ratios in terms of sin and cos when stuck.
Take care with square roots: for acute angles, sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot are all positive.

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from defining ratios and computing standard values through proving identities to solving practical elevation/depression problems. Work each one by identifying the type, drawing the triangle, and applying the appropriate ratio or identity.

keyPoints: The three primary ratios are sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent, remembered as SOH CAH TOA.
The reciprocal ratios are cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ.
The Pythagorean identities are sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ; dividing the first by sin² or cos² yields the other two.
Complementary-angle relationships: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ and sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ.
Standard values to memorise: sin 0° = 0, sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2, sin 90° = 1; cos θ follows the same table read backwards, and tan θ = sin θ/cos θ.
The angle of elevation is measured up from the observer's horizontal line, the angle of depression down from it, and when observer and object swap roles the two angles are equal alternate angles.
Height-and-distance problems almost always resolve through tan, because the unknown is usually the ratio of a vertical height to a horizontal distance.
For acute angles every ratio is positive, and each identity can be verified numerically at θ = 30°, 45° and 60° as a quick self-check.
examFocus: Draw and label the right triangle before writing any ratio; examiners award the setup mark on the labelled diagram even when the arithmetic slips.
State the identity you are using by name — complementary, Pythagorean or reciprocal — before applying it; the guess-and-substitute style loses method marks.
In elevation/depression questions, mark the horizontal line at the eye clearly; the angle is never measured from the ground unless the observer stands on it.
Keep exact surd forms (like 30√3) through the working and only convert to a decimal at the end; premature rounding loses accuracy marks.
For two-object depression questions, state which angle belongs to which object before computing distances; mixing the 60° line with the 45° point is the classic error.

vocabulary.meaning: The angle between the observer's horizontal line and the line of sight when the object is above the observer.
The angle between the observer's horizontal line and the line of sight when the object is below the observer.
Two angles whose sum is 90°; the sine, tangent and secant of one equal, respectively, the cosine, cotangent and cosecant of the other.
An equation true for every admissible value of the variable, such as sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, usable to replace one expression with another.
cosec, sec or cot — the reciprocal of a primary ratio; multiplying a ratio by its reciprocal gives 1.
The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle; the denominator of the sine and cosine ratios.
The straight line from the observer's eye to the object observed, which with the horizontal forms the elevation or depression angle.
An angle between 0° and 90°, within which all six trigonometric ratios are positive.

questions.prompt: If sin θ = 3/5 for an acute angle θ, then cos θ =
questions.explanation: For an acute angle the triangle has opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, so the adjacent side is √(5² − 3²) = 4 and cos θ = 4/5.
questions.commonMistake: Reading cos θ as sin θ / tan θ with the reciprocal ratios swapped, which gives 5/4 instead of 4/5.

questions.prompt: If sec θ + tan θ = 5, then sec θ − tan θ =
questions.explanation: The identity (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 holds for every θ, so the required value is 1/5.
questions.commonMistake: Adding rather than multiplying the conjugates, treating sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 as though it were a difference to evaluate.

questions.prompt: The value of tan 45° is:
questions.explanation: In the isosceles right triangle of a 45-45-90 triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are equal, so tan 45° = 1 exactly.
questions.commonMistake: Copying the standard-angle table row, for example taking √3/2 or 1/√2, which belong to 60° and 45°'s sine and cosine.

questions.prompt: The value of sin²30° + cos²30° is:
questions.explanation: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 holds for every angle, so the expression equals 1 exactly without any arithmetic on the 30° row of the table.
questions.commonMistake: Substituting √3/2 for both ratios and adding their squares to get 3/2, forgetting that the identity is exactly 1 for any θ.

questions.prompt: If tan θ = cot(2θ + 30°) for an acute angle θ, then θ =
questions.explanation: The complementary-angle identity says cot x = tan(90° − x). So tan θ = tan(90° − 2θ − 30°) = tan(60° − 2θ), giving θ = 60° − 2θ, so 3θ = 60° and θ = 20°.
questions.commonMistake: Equating cot x with tan(90° + x) instead of tan(90° − x), which yields an obtuse angle outside the acute range.

questions.prompt: A person stands at a horizontal distance from a tower equal to the tower's height. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower is:
questions.explanation: With opposite and adjacent sides equal (height = distance), tan θ = h/h = 1, so θ = 45°.
questions.commonMistake: Associating equal sides with the 30-60-90 special triangle rather than the isosceles right triangle that gives 45°.

questions.prompt: If sin(θ + 10°) = cos 40° for an acute angle θ, then θ =
questions.explanation: cos 40° = sin(90° − 40°) = sin 50° by the complementary identity. So θ + 10° = 50°, giving θ = 40°, which is acute as required.
questions.commonMistake: Setting θ + 10° = 40° directly, which treats the sine of an angle as equal to the cosine of the same angle rather than its complement.

questions.prompt: cosec²θ − cot²θ = ____ (the value of the left-hand side for every admissible θ).
questions.answer: 1 (this Pythagorean identity holds for every admissible θ)
questions.explanation: Dividing the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 through by sin²θ gives 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, and rearranging gives cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up the pair and writing cosec²θ − 1 = cot²θ with the wrong side, which is algebraically the same but frequently misapplied against sec/tan.

questions.prompt: sin θ x sec θ = ____.
questions.explanation: Since sec θ = 1/cos θ, the product is sin θ/cos θ, which is the definition of tan θ.
questions.commonMistake: Treating sec θ as 1/sin θ (the cosecant), which would give the product as 1 instead of tan θ.

questions.prompt: As the observer walks away from a tower along level ground, the angle of elevation of the tower's top ____.
questions.explanation: The angle of elevation satisfies tan θ = height/distance, and with the height fixed, increasing the distance reduces tan θ and hence θ; it tends towards 0° far away.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the geometry, since moving closer increases the angle; the words elevation and depression are the usual source of the mix-up.

questions.prompt: The angle of depression from a point above the ground to an object on the ground equals the angle of elevation from the object up to that point, because the two angles are ____ angles made by a horizontal pair.
questions.explanation: The observer's horizontal line and the ground's horizontal line are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal, so the depression and elevation angles are alternate and therefore equal.
questions.commonMistake: Labelling them vertically opposite angles; they are not, since they are measured between different pairs of lines at different points.

questions.prompt: cot θ is the ____ of tan θ.
questions.explanation: By definition cot θ = cos θ/sin θ = 1/tan θ, so the two ratios multiply to 1.
questions.commonMistake: Subtracting rather than reciprocating, which confuses cot θ with the negative of tan θ.

questions.prompt: Evaluate tan²45° + sin²30° − cos²60°.
questions.explanation: tan 45° = 1, sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 60° = 1/2. So the expression is 1 + 1/4 − 1/4 = 1 exactly. The sine and cosine terms cancel because sin 30° and cos 60° are complementary equals.
questions.commonMistake: Reading cos 60° as √3/2 (the 60° cosine belongs to 1/2), which would give 1 + 1/4 − 3/4 = 1/2 instead of the exact 1.

questions.prompt: Evaluate cosec 30° + sin 60°.
questions.commonMistake: Adding 2 and √3/2 as 2√3/2, which treats different surds as like terms.

questions.prompt: If sin θ = 12/13 with θ acute, find tan θ and sec θ.
questions.explanation: The right triangle has opposite 12 and hypotenuse 13, so the adjacent side is √(13² − 12²) = √(169 − 144) = 5. Then tan θ = 12/5 and sec θ = 1/cos θ = 13/5.
questions.commonMistake: Using the 3-4-5 shape (adjacent 5 but hypotenuse 12) and reporting sec 12/5, which mixes up the hypotenuse with a leg.

questions.prompt: Show that for any acute angle θ, (1 + sin θ)(1 − sin θ) simplifies to cos²θ.
questions.explanation: Expanding the product gives 1 − sin²θ. By the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ, which is the required simplification.
questions.commonMistake: Expanding to 1 + sin²θ (sign error) and then concluding incorrectly with sin²θ + cos²θ applied the wrong way.

questions.prompt: A tower stands on level ground. From a point 30 m from its foot, the angle of elevation of the top is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
questions.explanation: The right triangle has opposite = height and adjacent = 30 m, so tan 60° = h/30 and h = 30√3 ≈ 51.96 m, since tan 60° = √3 ≈ 1.732.
questions.commonMistake: Using tan 60° = 1/√3, which is the tan 30° value, and reporting the height as about 17.32 m.

questions.prompt: The complementary-angle identity pairs cot(90° − θ) with ____.
questions.explanation: The co-function identities convert each ratio into its complementary counterpart: cot(90° − θ) = tan θ, because cot x = tan(90° − x) applied with x = 90° − θ.
questions.commonMistake: Writing sec θ, which is the complement pair of cosec, not of cot.

questions.prompt: A man on a cliff 300 m high observes a boat on the sea below. The angle of depression of the boat is 30°. Find the horizontal distance of the boat from the foot of the cliff.
questions.explanation: The angle of depression 30° equals the angle of elevation from the boat. So tan 30° = 300/d, giving d = 300/tan 30° = 300√3 ≈ 519.6 m.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing 300 by √3 (which answers "height from distance") instead of multiplying, reversing opposite and adjacent.

questions.prompt: A ladder 25 m long leans against a wall and reaches a window 20 m above the ground. Find the distance of the foot of the ladder from the wall and the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
questions.answer: The foot is 15 m from the wall; the ladder makes an angle of about 53.1° with the ground (tan θ = 4/3)
questions.explanation: The wall, ground and ladder form a right triangle with hypotenuse 25 and one leg 20. The other leg is √(25² − 20²) = √(625 − 400) = 15 m, so the foot is 15 m from the wall. The inclination angle θ satisfies tan θ = 20/15 = 4/3 ≈ 1.333, and θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53.1°; equivalently sin θ = 20/25 = 0.8.
questions.commonMistake: Reporting the 15 m leg as the ladder's reach along the wall (that is the 20 m window height) or using sin θ = 15/25 with the legs swapped.

questions.prompt: From the top of a 7 m vertical pole, a bird spots two worms resting on the same straight level line on the ground on the same side of the pole. The angles of depression are 60° and 45°. Find the distance between the two worms.
questions.explanation: The angle of depression 45° corresponds to the farther point, which lies at a horizontal distance d1 = 7/tan 45° = 7 m from the foot. The angle of depression 60° corresponds to the nearer point, at d2 = 7/tan 60° = 7/√3 ≈ 4.04 m. Both are on the same side, so the separation is 7 − 7/√3 ≈ 2.96 m.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the two distances instead of subtracting them, which would be needed only if the objects were on opposite sides of the pole.

questions.prompt: A tower 20 m high stands on level ground, and a flagstaff of unknown height stands vertically on top of the tower. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of the tower's top is 30° and the angle of elevation of the flagstaff's top is 60°. Find the length of the flagstaff.
questions.explanation: Let d be the horizontal distance to the tower. Then tan 30° = 20/d, so d = 20/tan 30° = 20√3. The flag top accounts for the whole angle of elevation: tan 60° = (20 + f)/d, so (20 + f) = 20√3 x √3 = 60, giving f = 40 m. Check: the flagstaff is 40 m and the tower is 20 m, so the flag height above the tower is exactly twice the visible tower, consistent with the 30°/60° doubling pattern.
questions.commonMistake: Setting tan 60° = f/d rather than (20 + f)/d, which ignores that the 60° line reaches past the tower section before the flagstaff.

questions.prompt: If tan θ + cot θ = 2 for an acute angle θ, find θ and verify that sin θ = cos θ for that value.
questions.explanation: Let t = tan θ. Then cot θ = 1/t, so t + 1/t = 2. Multiplying by t: t² + 1 = 2t, so t² − 2t + 1 = (t − 1)² = 0, giving t = 1 and θ = 45°. Verification: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, which is exactly the special triangle's isosceles property reflecting tan 45° = 1.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing by t instead of rearranging as a perfect square, which loses one of the roots and hides that the equation has the single acute solution 45°.
